section.title: Jacob Blesses Ephraim and Manasseh
section.sectionRationale: The dying Jacob rallies to adopt Joseph's two Egyptian-born sons as his own and to bless them. With crossed hands he deliberately sets the younger Ephraim above the elder Manasseh, once again overturning human expectation, and he blesses in the name of the God who has shepherded and redeemed him all his life.
section.thesis: As Jacob adopts and blesses Ephraim and Manasseh, God's freedom to elevate the younger and His faithfulness as shepherd and redeemer are put on display, carrying the covenant promise into the next generation.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: Jacob adopts Joseph's sons and recalls the covenant; the crossed hands and the blessing of the God who shepherds and redeems; and the younger set before the elder with a word of God's future faithfulness.

units.label: Jacob adopts Joseph's sons
units.note: they shall be reckoned as mine

verses.text: Some time later Joseph was told, “Your father is ill.” So he set out with his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.
When Jacob was told, “Your son Joseph has come to you,” Israel rallied his strength and sat up in bed.
Jacob said to Joseph, “{{elshaddai|God Almighty}} appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and there He blessed me
and told me, ‘Behold, I will make you fruitful and multiply you; I will make you a multitude of peoples, and will give this land to your descendants after you as an everlasting possession.’
And now your two sons born to you in Egypt before I came to you here shall be reckoned as mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine.
Any children born to you after them shall be yours, and they shall be called by the names of their brothers in the territory they inherit.

Now as for me, when I was returning from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died along the way in the land of Canaan, some distance from Ephrath. So I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath” (that is, Bethlehem).

units.label: The crossed hands
units.note: the God who has been my shepherd

verses.text: When Israel saw the sons of Joseph, he asked, “Who are these?”
Joseph said to his father, “They are the sons God has given me in this place.” So Jacob said, “Please bring them to me, that I may {{barak|bless}} them.”
Now Israel’s eyesight was poor because of old age; he could hardly see. Joseph brought his sons to him, and his father kissed them and embraced them.
“I never expected to see your face again,” Israel said to Joseph, “but now God has let me see your children as well.”
Then Joseph removed his sons from his father’s knees and bowed facedown.
And Joseph took both of them, with Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand, and brought them close to him.
But Israel stretched out his right hand and put it on the head of Ephraim, the younger; and crossing his hands, he put his left on Manasseh’s head, although Manasseh was the {{bekor|firstborn}}.
Then he blessed Joseph and said: “May the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day,

the angel who has {{gaal|redeemed}} me from all harm, may He bless these boys. And may they be called by my name and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth.”
When Joseph saw that his father had placed his right hand on Ephraim’s head, he was displeased and took his father’s hand to move it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s.
“Not so, my father!” Joseph said. “This one is the firstborn; put your right hand on his head.”

But his father refused. “I know, my son, I know!” he said. “He too shall become a people, and he too shall be great; nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations.”
So that day Jacob blessed them and said: “By you shall Israel pronounce this blessing: ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.’” So he put Ephraim before Manasseh.
Then Israel said to Joseph, “Look, I am about to die, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers.
And to you, as one who is above your brothers, I give the ridge of land that I took from the Amorites with my sword and bow.”

elshaddai.gloss: God Almighty, the name by which God appeared to the patriarchs with promises of fruitfulness and land. Jacob recalls this appearance at Luz as the ground of the blessing he now passes on. The name anchors the whole scene in the covenant God made with Abraham and Isaac.

barak.gloss: To bless, to speak favor and God's good gifts over another. Jacob's dying act is to bless, transmitting the covenant blessing to a new generation. In Scripture such blessing is not mere well-wishing but a powerful word tied to God's purpose.

gaal.gloss: To redeem, to act as a kinsman who rescues and buys back. Jacob calls God the angel who has redeemed him from all harm. The word looks ahead to God as the great Redeemer of His people, ultimately in Christ.

bekor.gloss: The firstborn, who by custom held the chief inheritance and rank. Jacob crosses his hands to put the younger before the firstborn, as God had done with Jacob himself. The word highlights how God's choice repeatedly overturns human precedence.

basic.context: The dying Jacob adopts Joseph's two Egyptian-born sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, as his own, giving Joseph a double portion. Then, with crossed hands, he blesses the younger above the elder. The key question is why Jacob deliberately reverses the expected order of the firstborn.
basic.hermeneutics: This is narrative that turns on a deliberate, Spirit-guided act: the crossing of the hands. The main question is whether Jacob has simply made a mistake because of his blindness. The text is clear that he knows exactly what he is doing.
basic.originalLanguages: Jacob invokes El Shaddai, God Almighty, the covenant name, and blesses, barak, the boys. He names God as the one who has been his shepherd and the angel who has redeemed, gaal, him. Though Manasseh is the bekor, the firstborn, God's choice again elevates the younger.
basic.typology: The pattern of the younger chosen over the elder runs through Genesis and points beyond merit to grace. Jacob names God as his shepherd and redeemer, titles fulfilled in Christ the good Shepherd and the true Redeemer of His people.
basic.christ: Jacob blesses in the name of the God who shepherded and redeemed him, longing that his sons be gathered under the same care. Both titles find their fullness in Jesus, the Shepherd who lays down His life and the Redeemer who buys His people back from all harm.
basic.god: God is praised as the covenant-keeping Almighty, the lifelong shepherd, and the redeemer from all harm. He is free to bless as He chooses, lifting the younger above the elder by grace. His faithfulness spans the generations from Abraham to these boys.
basic.crossReferences: The younger-over-elder pattern echoes Isaac over Ishmael and Jacob over Esau. Ephraim's elevation shapes later Israelite history, and the shepherd and redeemer titles flower in Psalm 23 and in Christ.
basic.oneStory: The covenant blessing is handed down to a new generation, and the tribes of Israel take shape. God's gracious freedom and covenant faithfulness carry the promise forward toward the nation and the Messiah.

context.literary:
Genesis 48 is the first of two deathbed scenes, and it is written to be read against an earlier one. In Genesis 27 an old father whose eyes 'were so weak that he could no longer see,' Genesis 27:1, asked, 'Which one are you, my son?' Genesis 27:18, and was tricked into blessing the younger son over the elder. Now the deceiver of that scene is the old man with failing eyes, verse 10, and he asks, 'Who are these?' verse 8. Once again the younger is blessed above the elder, but this time no one is deceived. The one who blesses knows exactly what he is doing, and it is the father of the boys who protests.

The chapter moves in three steps. Jacob first grounds everything in God's word at Luz, verses 3 and 4, then adopts Joseph's two sons, verses 5 and 6, and explains himself with a sorrowful memory of Rachel, verse 7. The middle scene is staged with great care. Joseph positions the boys so that Manasseh will stand at Jacob's right hand, verse 13, and Jacob deliberately crosses his arms, verse 14. The blessing that follows, verses 15 and 16, is a small poem in three lines about God: the God before whom his fathers walked, the God who shepherded him, and the angel who redeemed him. The last scene brings Joseph's objection, Jacob's refusal, a blessing formula for later Israel, and a closing word about the land, verses 17 to 22.

The chapter gathers up one of Genesis's great patterns. Abel's offering was accepted over Cain's, Genesis 4:4-5; Isaac was chosen over Ishmael; Jacob over Esau, Genesis 25:23; Perez broke out ahead of Zerah, Genesis 38:29; Joseph was raised above his older brothers. Ephraim over Manasseh is the last example in the book, and the clearest case of the reversal being enacted openly in a blessing with full knowledge.
context.historical:
The chronology helps. Joseph's sons were born before the famine, Genesis 41:50, and Jacob has now lived seventeen years in Egypt, Genesis 47:28. Ephraim and Manasseh are therefore young men, not small children. When Joseph removes them 'from his father's knees,' verse 12, the gesture is formal. The knees were a place of acknowledgement and adoption: Rachel spoke of Bilhah bearing children, literally, 'on my knees,' Genesis 30:3, and later the sons of Machir 'were brought up on Joseph's knees,' Genesis 50:23.

Jacob's words 'Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine,' verse 5, are an adoption. He names his own two eldest sons as the standard. The effect is to give Joseph a double share in the inheritance through his sons, the portion that belonged to the firstborn, Deuteronomy 21:17. The Chronicler states the result plainly: Reuben's 'birthright was given to the sons of Joseph son of Israel, because Reuben defiled his father's bed,' 1 Chronicles 5:1, referring to Genesis 35:22 and 49:3-4. Joseph, Rachel's firstborn, receives the firstborn's portion.

The mention of Rachel's grave, verse 7, is not a stray memory. Rachel died on the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem, Genesis 35:19, giving birth to her second son. By adopting her grandsons as his own sons, Jacob gives Rachel, in effect, the further children she did not live to bear.

The adoption shaped Israel's tribal map. 'The descendants of Joseph became two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim,' Joshua 14:4, while Levi received no territory, so that twelve tribes still divided the land. Ephraim's later prominence was real. Joshua was an Ephraimite, Numbers 13:8, the tabernacle stood at Shiloh in Ephraim's territory, Joshua 18:1, and Jeroboam, first king of the northern kingdom, was 'an Ephraimite,' 1 Kings 11:26. By the time of the prophets the name Ephraim could stand for the whole north, Isaiah 7:2. Precedence did not always mean numbers: Ephraim outnumbered Manasseh in the first census, Numbers 1:33-35, but Manasseh was larger in the second, Numbers 26:34-37.
context.canonical:
The chapter's language about God passes into Israel's worship. Jacob's confession of 'the God who has been my shepherd' returns in the next chapter as 'the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel,' Genesis 49:24, and Psalm 80 prays in words that could have been drawn from this scene: 'Hear us, O Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph like a flock,' with a plea that God would shine forth 'before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh,' Psalm 80:1-2, the three tribes that came from Rachel. Psalm 23:1 gives the confession its most familiar form.

Ephraim's precedence is both confirmed and qualified later. Moses' blessing speaks of 'the myriads of Ephraim' and 'the thousands of Manasseh,' Deuteronomy 33:17, keeping the order of Genesis 48:20. Jeremiah calls Ephraim God's firstborn, Jeremiah 31:9, and 'a precious son,' Jeremiah 31:20. Yet Psalm 78 records that God 'refused the tribe of Ephraim' and 'chose the tribe of Judah,' Psalm 78:67-68, for the kingship. Ezekiel pictures the stick of Joseph 'in the hand of Ephraim' joined to the stick of Judah so that they become one in God's hand, Ezekiel 37:19.

The memory of Rachel at Bethlehem also travels. Jeremiah hears 'Rachel weeping for her children' at Ramah, Jeremiah 31:15, and Matthew applies the verse to the mourning at Bethlehem after Jesus' birth, Matthew 2:18.

In the New Testament, Hebrews singles out this very scene: 'By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph's sons,' Hebrews 11:21. Paul uses the pattern of the younger chosen over the elder to explain that God's purpose stands 'not by works but by Him who calls,' Romans 9:11-12. And John records that Jesus met the Samaritan woman 'near the plot of ground that Jacob had given to his son Joseph,' John 4:5, the portion of Genesis 48:22, where Joseph's bones were buried, Joshua 24:32.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand why their tribal list included Ephraim and Manasseh rather than a single tribe of Joseph, and why Ephraim stood ahead of his older brother. The answer is that the patriarch, speaking in God's name, made it so. The tribal order was not an accident of history but the outworking of a blessing given before Israel ever entered the land.

More deeply, the chapter wanted Israel to see that God's choice follows His own purpose rather than human rules of rank. Israel itself took its name from a younger son, and Moses would later remind them that the LORD did not choose them 'because you were more numerous than the other peoples,' Deuteronomy 7:7. Ephraim's elevation, like Jacob's own, was a lesson in grace.

Finally, the chapter gives Israel a confession to live by. Jacob sums up his whole troubled life in three phrases about God: the God of his fathers, his shepherd all his life, the angel who redeemed him from all harm, verses 15 and 16. That is how Moses wanted Israel to read their own history in the wilderness: not as a series of accidents and hardships but as a journey under the care of a Shepherd who redeems.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a patriarch's adoption and blessing of his grandsons. It does not set up crossed hands or the laying of hands on the young as a required ritual, nor does it overturn the ordinary honour due to the firstborn in family life, which the law later protected, Deuteronomy 21:15-17. Jacob's authority to reverse the order came from his role as the bearer of God's covenant blessing, and he acts in knowledge that goes beyond ordinary judgment, verse 19.

What does carry forward is the practice of blessing the next generation in God's name, which Israel continued in the words of verse 20, 'May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.' Jewish families still use those words in blessing their sons. Christians too may speak God's blessing over children, as Jesus did when He 'placed His hands on them, and blessed them,' Mark 10:16. And the chapter's confession of God as shepherd and redeemer is a model for how believers can interpret their own lives before their children, telling of the God who has kept them.

debates.question: Who is 'the angel who has redeemed me from all harm' in verse 16?

views.label: God Himself, the Angel of the LORD
views.case: The three lines of verses 15 and 16 are parallel, and the verb that follows, 'may He bless,' is singular, so the angel is identified with God. Jacob had met 'the angel of God' who said, 'I am the God of Bethel,' Genesis 31:11-13, and Hosea says he 'struggled with the angel,' Hosea 12:4, the one Jacob said was God, Genesis 32:30. Many church fathers saw here an appearance of the Son before the incarnation. The BSB footnote allows 'Angel.'

views.label: A created angel sent by God
views.case: Others read the angel as a messenger distinct from God, such as the angel God sent before Abraham's servant, Genesis 24:40, through whom God's protection came. On this view Jacob prays that God and His agent together will bless the boys.

views.label: A poetic way of naming God's providence
views.case: A third view treats 'angel' as a poetic parallel for God's protective care, without deciding the question of a distinct figure, and focuses on the confession that God has rescued Jacob.

debates.bearing: The singular verb and Jacob's own history favour the first view. Isaiah later speaks of 'the Angel of His Presence' who saved Israel and of God who 'redeemed them,' Isaiah 63:9, holding the angel and God together in the same way.

debates.question: What is the 'ridge of land' Jacob took 'with my sword and bow' in verse 22?

views.label: Shechem, taken by his sons
views.case: The BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew shekem sounds like Shechem. Jacob had bought land there, Genesis 33:19, and Simeon and Levi had seized the city with the sword, Genesis 34:25-29. On this view Jacob claims their action as the family's, though he had condemned it, Genesis 34:30.

views.label: An event Genesis does not record
views.case: Others think Jacob refers to a conflict with Amorites not narrated elsewhere, since Genesis 34 is a massacre he denounced rather than a victory he would boast of.

views.label: A prophetic claim
views.case: Some take the verb as a confident statement about the future conquest, when Joseph's descendants would hold Shechem, as they did, Joshua 24:32.

debates.bearing: Whatever the event, the gift was real. Joseph's bones were buried at Shechem, and John 4:5 still calls it 'the plot of ground that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.'

debates.question: What does the verb translated 'crossing his hands' in verse 14 mean?

views.label: He crossed his arms
views.case: Most translations take the verb to describe the physical action, since Jacob reaches his right hand across to the younger boy on his left. This fits the staging of verse 13 exactly.

views.label: He acted deliberately
views.case: The verb sakal usually means to act wisely or with insight. Some render the clause 'he guided his hands knowingly,' stressing that the crossing was intentional, which verse 19, 'I know, my son, I know,' confirms.

debates.bearing: The two meanings describe one act from two angles. Jacob's hands crossed, and they crossed because he knew what he was doing.

study.originalLanguages:
Jacob's blessing in verses 15 and 16 is a small poem in three lines, each describing God by a participle or a relative clause. The first line speaks of 'the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked,' using the reflexive form of halak, to walk about, live one's life. It is the verb of God's charge to Abram, 'Walk before Me and be blameless,' Genesis 17:1, and of Abraham's own testimony, 'The LORD, before whom I have walked,' Genesis 24:40. To walk before God is to live openly in His presence.

The second line says, literally, 'the God who has been shepherding me from my being until this day.' The participle is from raah, to pasture, to shepherd. This is the first time in the Bible that God is called a shepherd. Jacob knew the work from the inside; he had told Laban, 'I will keep on shepherding,' Genesis 30:31, and described the heat by day and frost by night he endured for the flocks, Genesis 31:38-40. Now at the end of his life he says God did that for him. The title returns in Genesis 49:24 and becomes a central image of God in Psalm 23:1 and Psalm 80:1.

The third line calls God 'the angel who has redeemed me from all harm.' The word malak means messenger, and the BSB footnote allows 'Angel.' What follows is striking: after three descriptions, the verb is singular, 'may He bless these boys.' The grammar makes the God of the fathers, the shepherd and the angel one subject. The verb goel, redeemer, appears here for the first time in Scripture. It belongs to the kinsman who buys back what a relative has lost, and God takes it up for Himself at the exodus, 'I will redeem you with an outstretched arm,' Exodus 6:6.

In verse 4 Jacob recalls God's promise to make him 'a multitude of peoples,' qehal ammim. The noun qahal means an assembly, a gathered company. It echoes Isaac's blessing, 'a company of peoples,' Genesis 28:3, and God's word at Bethel, 'a company of nations,' Genesis 35:11. The same noun later names the assembly of Israel gathered before the LORD.

In verse 19 Jacob says Ephraim's offspring will become 'a multitude of nations,' literally 'the fullness of the nations,' melo haggoyim. Some readers hear an anticipation of Paul's 'the full number of the Gentiles,' Romans 11:25, though Paul does not cite this verse, and the link should be held lightly.

Finally, Jacob's refusal in verse 19 repeats the verb yada, to know: 'I know, my son, I know.' The doubling answers Joseph's assumption that his father's blindness has led him astray. The one who once exploited his own father's blindness now insists that his dim eyes see what his son cannot.

typology.type: The younger set before the firstborn, Genesis 48:14-20
typology.fulfillment: Jacob's crossed hands enact God's freedom to choose apart from rank, the pattern Paul traces to show that God's purpose stands 'not by works but by Him who calls,' Romans 9:11-12. In Christ the pattern widens: God 'chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong,' 1 Corinthians 1:27, and Gentiles once far off become 'members of God's household,' Ephesians 2:19. The type falls short in the later history of Ephraim, whose privilege turned to pride and quarrelling, Judges 12:1 and Psalm 78:9. Grace in Christ produces humility, not rivalry.

typology.type: God my shepherd all my life, Genesis 48:15
typology.fulfillment: Jacob, a shepherd himself, confesses that God has shepherded him through every hardship. Jesus claims the title and deepens it: 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11. Peter tells believers that they have 'returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls,' 1 Peter 2:25. The escalation lies in the cost. Jacob's God guided and protected him; in Christ the Shepherd dies for the flock.

typology.type: The angel who redeemed me from all harm, Genesis 48:16
typology.fulfillment: Jacob names the divine messenger who rescued him and prays that the same one will bless the boys. The New Testament presents Christ as the One sent from the Father who redeems: God 'sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law,' Galatians 4:4-5, and 'He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness,' Titus 2:14. Jacob was redeemed from harms in this life. Christ redeems from sin itself, and at the price of His own blood.

typology.type: Egyptian born sons adopted into Israel, Genesis 48:5
typology.fulfillment: Ephraim and Manasseh were born in Egypt to an Egyptian mother, Genesis 41:50, yet Jacob says, 'they shall be mine,' giving them full standing among his sons and a share in the land. Believers are adopted in the same way: God 'predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ,' Ephesians 1:5, and 'if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed and heirs,' Galatians 3:29. Jacob's adoption gave territory in Canaan; God's gives an eternal inheritance.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the titles Jacob gives to God. He calls God his shepherd, the first time Scripture uses that image of God, and the Shepherd of Israel becomes one of the Old Testament's great hopes. The prophets promised that God would shepherd His people Himself, 'I will tend My flock,' Ezekiel 34:15, and Matthew applies to Jesus the word about Bethlehem, 'out of you will come a ruler who will be the shepherd of My people Israel,' Matthew 2:6. Jesus says, 'I am the good shepherd,' John 10:11, and He adds what Jacob could not have foreseen: this shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.

It leads to Christ through the angel who redeems. Jacob identifies the angel with God and asks Him to bless. Whether or not Jacob's angel was the Son appearing before the incarnation, as many in the early church believed, the New Testament shows the reality to which the title points: the One sent from the Father to redeem, Galatians 4:4-5, who gave Himself 'to redeem us from all lawlessness,' Titus 2:14. Jacob was redeemed 'from all harm'; Christ redeems from the root of all harm.

It leads to Christ through adoption. Jacob takes two young men born in Egypt, sons of an Egyptian mother, and makes them full heirs with his own sons. The gospel does the same on a larger scale. Those who were strangers are made 'fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household,' Ephesians 2:19, and receive 'adoption as sons,' Galatians 4:5. Like Ephraim and Manasseh, they are called by a new family name.

It leads to Christ through the pattern of grace. The younger is set above the elder, not because of merit or strength, but because the one who blesses chooses. Jesus' ministry was full of such reversals. He said the last would be first, welcomed children, and gave the kingdom to those the world overlooked. In Him God's free choice is not arbitrary but gracious, gathering those who have no claim.

Finally, the scene of a departing father blessing with his hands has an echo in the Gospels. Jesus laid His hands on children and blessed them, Mark 10:16. And at His ascension, 'He lifted up His hands and blessed them,' and while He was blessing them He was carried up into heaven, Luke 24:50-51. Jacob blessed and then died; Christ blesses and reigns, and His blessing rests on His people permanently. These links rest on the New Testament's own titles and patterns; the crossed hands themselves are not a hidden picture of the cross, and should not be pressed into one.
study.god:
Jacob's blessing in verses 15 and 16 is a summary of a whole life's theology, and they show God in three ways. He is the God of the fathers, the one before whom Abraham and Isaac walked. God's faithfulness is generational. He does not begin afresh with each person but carries a promise from one life to the next, and Jacob now hands that promise on to boys who were born in Egypt.

He is the God who shepherds. Jacob's life had been hard, as he told Pharaoh, Genesis 47:9: flight from Esau, twenty years of labour under Laban, the loss of Rachel, the long grief for Joseph. Looking back, he does not say God kept him from hardship. He says God shepherded him through it 'all my life to this day.' The shepherd image holds together God's guidance, provision and protection, and it shows a God who stays close to the ones He leads.

He is the God who redeems. The angel who 'redeemed me from all harm' takes the role of a kinsman who rescues his own. God attaches Himself to His people so closely that their losses become His to restore. Isaiah draws the same picture: 'In all their distress, He too was afflicted, and the Angel of His Presence saved them,' Isaiah 63:9.

The chapter also shows God's sovereign freedom. God Almighty had promised Jacob fruitfulness, verse 4, and now, through Jacob's crossed hands, He decides how that fruitfulness will be distributed. Ephraim, whose very name means that 'God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction,' Genesis 41:52, receives the greater share. God is not bound by birth order, custom or even the wishes of Joseph, the most honoured of the sons. His choices are His own.

Yet His freedom is not coldness. Manasseh is not rejected: 'He too shall become a people, and he too shall be great,' verse 19. God's choice of one is not contempt for the other. And Jacob's final word to Joseph shows the character of the God he has known: 'I am about to die, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers,' verse 21. Human leaders die; God remains, and His promise goes on.

For worship, Jacob's confession is a pattern. At the end of a hard life he speaks of God with gratitude, not complaint. He names God by what God has done for him, and he asks that the same God would bless those who come after him. Believers who look back on their own lives are invited to confess the same Shepherd and Redeemer.

crossReferences.note: Blind Isaac asked, 'Which one are you, my son?' and was deceived into blessing the younger. Genesis 48:8 repeats the scene with Jacob as the old man asking, 'Who are these?' This time the younger is blessed above the elder knowingly. The deceiver has become the one who blesses in truth.

Joseph named Manasseh because God had made him forget his hardship, and Ephraim because God had made him fruitful in the land of his affliction. Jacob's blessing on Ephraim fulfils the meaning of the younger son's name, since his offspring will become a multitude.

At Bethel God Almighty renamed Jacob Israel and promised fruitfulness, 'a company of nations,' and the land. Genesis 48:3-4 recalls this very appearance. Jacob grounds the adoption and blessing in God's word, not in his own preference.

Reuben's birthright 'was given to the sons of Joseph,' because Reuben defiled his father's bed, though the ruler came from Judah. The Chronicler explains the result of Genesis 48:5: Joseph received the firstborn's double share through Ephraim and Manasseh.

In his blessing of Joseph, Jacob speaks of 'the Mighty One of Jacob' and 'the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel.' The shepherd title first used of God in Genesis 48:15 returns at once, now linked with strength and stability for Joseph's descendants.

'Hear us, O Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph like a flock,' and shine forth 'before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh.' The psalmist prays for the tribes descended from Rachel using the very title Jacob gave God as he blessed Ephraim and Manasseh.

'The Angel of His Presence saved them. In His love and compassion He redeemed them.' Isaiah joins the angel and redemption as Genesis 48:16 does, and presents both as God's own saving presence with His people throughout their history.

God says, 'Ephraim is My firstborn.' The younger son whom Jacob set ahead of his brother is taken up as the name for the northern tribes, and God declares a father's love for them even after their exile, carrying Jacob's blessing into the prophets' hope.

God 'refused the tribe of Ephraim' and 'chose the tribe of Judah' for the throne. The precedence Ephraim received in Genesis 48 did not include kingship, which belonged to Judah, Genesis 49:10. Ephraim's blessing was real but bounded.

'By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph's sons.' Hebrews treats the scene of Genesis 48 as an act of faith. Jacob gave his grandsons a share in a land none of them yet possessed, trusting God's promise beyond his own death.

Paul explains that God's plan of election stands 'not by works but by Him who calls,' citing Jacob and Esau. The same principle governs Ephraim's elevation in Genesis 48:19, and Paul makes it the basis of grace for Jew and Gentile alike.

Jesus came to Sychar 'near the plot of ground that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.' The gift of Genesis 48:22 was still remembered in Jesus' day, and there He offered living water to a Samaritan woman whose people called Jacob 'our father,' John 4:12.

study.oneStory:
The first blessing in the Bible was God's word to humanity, 'Be fruitful and multiply,' Genesis 1:28. After the fall that blessing narrowed to a promise given to Abraham and carried from father to son. Genesis 48 is one of the last handings on of that blessing in the patriarchal story. Jacob, who fought for a blessing all his life, now gives one freely, and he gives it in the name of the God who first spoke it.

The chapter answers questions raised earlier in Genesis. Why was the younger so often chosen? Because God's purpose runs on grace, not on rank. What would become of Joseph, the son who was lost and found? He receives the double portion, and Rachel, who died on the road to Bethlehem, is honoured in the adoption of her grandsons. What had God been doing through all of Jacob's hard years? Shepherding and redeeming him.

The chapter also looks ahead. It shapes the tribes that will enter the land, gives Ephraim the prominence that will mark Israel's history, and ends with a promise: 'God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers,' verse 21. That promise becomes the exodus. The names of Ephraim and Manasseh will be spoken over Israel's children for generations, verse 20.

The story finds its centre in Christ. He is the good Shepherd Jacob confessed and the Redeemer Jacob named. Through Him the blessing given to Abraham reaches those born far from the land, as Ephraim and Manasseh were born in Egypt, and they are adopted as sons and called by His name. The divided tribes of Ephraim and Judah, whom Ezekiel saw joined into one stick in God's hand, Ezekiel 37:19, become one flock under one Shepherd.

In the new creation the Lamb at the centre of the throne 'will be their shepherd,' leading them to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17. The blessing Jacob spoke over two boys in Egypt, that they would grow into a multitude upon the earth, will be fulfilled in 'a multitude too large to count,' Revelation 7:9, gathered from every nation under the name of the God who shepherds and redeems.

quiz.q: What does Jacob do with Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh?

options.text: He adopts them as his own, granting Joseph a double portion, and blesses them.
options.note: Reckoning them as his own gives Joseph a double inheritance through them.

options.text: He sends them away because they were born in Egypt.
options.note: The opposite; he embraces them and claims them as his own sons.

options.text: He refuses to acknowledge them at all.
options.note: He gladly receives them, saying God has let him see Joseph's children.

options.text: He gives them to Pharaoh to raise.
options.note: He keeps them within the covenant family and blesses them.

quiz.q: What is significant about Jacob crossing his hands during the blessing?

options.text: He deliberately sets the younger Ephraim above the elder Manasseh.
options.note: God's choice again overturns the expected order of the firstborn.

options.text: He simply could not see which boy was which.
options.note: Joseph thinks so, but Jacob says I know, my son, I know; the act is intentional.

options.text: He was blessing only one of the two boys.
options.note: He blesses both, but places the younger first.

options.text: He accidentally blessed Joseph instead of the sons.
options.note: He knowingly blesses the boys, hands crossed on purpose.

quiz.q: How does Jacob describe God in his blessing?

options.text: As his lifelong shepherd and the angel who has redeemed him from all harm.
options.note: These titles point ahead to Christ the Shepherd and Redeemer.

options.text: As a distant God who left him to fend for himself.
options.note: The opposite; Jacob confesses God's constant care and rescue.

options.text: As a God he has only just come to know.
options.note: He speaks of God's care all my life to this day.

options.text: As a God who blesses only the strong and firstborn.
options.note: The blessing highlights grace to the younger, not the strong.

quiz.q: How does Joseph react to the crossed hands, and how does Jacob answer?

options.text: Joseph tries to correct it; Jacob refuses, saying the younger will be greater.
options.note: Jacob knowingly upholds God's choice of Ephraim.

options.text: Joseph approves at once and says nothing.
options.note: Joseph is actually displeased and tries to move his father's hand.

options.text: Jacob apologizes and switches his hands.
options.note: Jacob refuses to switch; he acts with full intent.

options.text: Joseph removes his sons in anger.
options.note: Joseph objects but does not withdraw them; the blessing stands.

quiz.q: What larger biblical pattern does this scene illustrate?

options.text: God's gracious freedom to choose and bless apart from human precedence.
options.note: As with Jacob over Esau, God elevates the younger by grace.

options.text: That the firstborn always receives the greater blessing.
options.note: The scene overturns exactly that expectation.

options.text: That blessings depend on a father's eyesight.
options.note: Jacob's blindness is noted, but the choice is deliberate, not accidental.

options.text: That God's promises had come to an end.
options.note: The blessing carries the covenant promise forward to a new generation.

questions: Jacob looked back over his whole life and called God his shepherd. As you look back over yours, where can you trace God's shepherding care?
God repeatedly chose the younger, the overlooked, the unexpected. How does it encourage you that God's blessing runs on grace rather than rank or merit?
Jacob called God the one who redeemed him from all harm. What harm has God brought you through that you can name and give thanks for?
Near death, Jacob's great concern was to pass on blessing to the next generation. Whom are you called to bless and speak God's good over?
Joseph wanted the blessing to follow his own plan, but God's choice differed. Where might you need to release your expectations and trust God's way?

translationNotes.note: Paddan is short for Paddan-aram, that is, northwest Mesopotamia; Jacob recalls Rachel's death near Ephrath, which the text identifies as Bethlehem.
The angel who has redeemed me uses the kinsman-redeemer language, gaal; the same word underlies the great biblical theme of God as Redeemer of His people.
The word rendered ridge of land is shekem, which sounds like the town and district of Shechem; the phrase can also be read as one portion above your brothers.
